caption: A guest room fit for royalty — Rajasthan, India. Wrapped in gold from floor to ceiling, and still, it feels almost bare. Makes you wonder what royalty really looked like back then, if this was the minimum.
The palace doesn't end where your eye tells you it should. Sandstone, carved inch by inch, precise enough to make you forget it's stone at all. Rajasthan, India.
Didn't know the name, didn't need to — the light and the wind did all the talking. A friend later told me: Kaash Phool. Some frames earn their place before you even understand what you're looking at.

Rain was pouring during the Bannerghatta safari when I spotted him — a big fellow, clearly enjoying the downpour, but the moment he noticed the camera, he tried to shrink behind a tree. Playful and shy, all in the same breath.
Didn't know the name, didn't need to — the attitude alone earned the shot. My first bird shot ever: a Red-whiskered Bulbul. Kodaikanal, Tamil Nadu.
Another face of Rajasthan — this time in marble. A temple built with the same devotion as the palaces, except here, the grandeur was never meant for royalty. It was for something bigger.

This tree was dry, almost dead — but nature had one more moment saved up for it. Against a sky washed pink, its bare black branches looked less like decay and more like a painting drawn straight from the heavens.
This bulb looked ordinary, nothing worth a second glance — until a small shower rolled in and the light bent through it, throwing out a streak of green. Suddenly, plain wasn't the word anymore.
The mountain in Kodaikanal barely revealed itself that day, half-swallowed by fog, the sky heavy with cloud. No color needed — black and white said everything.
Met this leopard during the Bannerghatta safari — quiet, watchful, and completely at ease in its own skin. Some animals are built to perform. This one was built to just be itself.
It was a rainy day on my Kodaikanal trip, bikes crowded together, everything soaked and dull under the grey. But this one still outshined the rest — like the weather couldn't touch it.

The closer I looked, the more it stopped feeling like a photograph and started feeling like proof — of just how perfectly, sophisticatedly engineered the human eye really is. Nothing man-made comes close.

This tree always finds me at the same time every year — lights, tinsel, that same warm glow — and somehow it never comes alone. It brings the people I miss badly, and the smell of fresh-baked cookies I still crave.
The butterfly and the flower bud always seem to find each other. I shot this in black and white, but somehow it's still one of the most colorful frames I own — just not in the way you'd expect.

The leaves are nature — the root cause, the origin of everything that gets built afterward. And there, tangled right into them, hangs a bulb — something so basic now, we forget it was ever built at all.

Just an Apsara pencil, really — but split between silver that throws the light back and black that eats it completely. Stacked together like this, it stops looking real. The eye can't quite decide what it's seeing.

This beach always drags me back to childhood — playful evenings, half land and half water, and that line where the sky just gives in to the sea. Doesn't matter where or when — a frame like this is always worth taking.

The thorns stand out sharp in this frame, almost too clear to ignore. But if you've ever wondered why a plant grows them in the first place — it's not without reason. Somewhere in its past, something taught it to protect itself.

This rock has circled us forever, always showing the same face, still looking clear and whole from here. It made me wonder — every rock on Earth probably looked just like this once, before human hands ever broke one down.

I keep trying to find the right words for this one and I still can't. It's only a watchtower on a fort wall — nothing more, nothing dramatic — and yet the way it was built, every arch stacked on arch, every carving placed like it mattered, left me standing there in complete silence. Some things you don't photograph because you understand them. You photograph them because you don't.

There was a strange familiarity the second I saw him — like my brain had already lived this frame once before. Not through him, but through a version of myself I hadn't thought about in years. The energy, the cheerfulness, that habit of finding joy in absolutely everything, with no walls and no boundaries to keep it in. Seeing him standing there brought all of it back.

Another one from Rajasthan — and honestly, I stopped trying to look for the "right" shot after a while. Every random view, every accidental glance out of a window, felt like it deserved to be framed. This one just happened to be in front of me.

This was my first love — the first piece of equipment that made me feel whole, that gave me an identity I didn't have before it. Everything after this started because of this camera. It'll always hold a special place — in this gallery, in my heart, everywhere.

This looked like just another nice sunset frame from Gokarna until it hit me — the dry grass, the lone tree, that faded desert light — this could've been ripped straight out of Breaking Bad. Didn't expect a trip to the coast to end up looking like New Mexico.

The ocean was so bright it nearly swallowed the sky, standing in contrast to the quiet land behind them — a father and his son, just watching. I know this sounds strange, but I'd seen this exact frame in a dream long before I stood here. All I had to do was wait for it to catch up to me.

Another frame from Rajasthan — this one built itself, really. The arch I stood under happened to frame the one across from it perfectly, both carved from the same sandstone. Whoever designed these back then clearly had an eye for it — this kind of taste doesn't happen by accident.

There was something about this courtyard that felt oddly familiar — the sun-bleached walls, the old wooden shutters, the quiet of it all. It took me a second to place it: this looked exactly like a picture straight out of my history textbook. Except this time, I wasn't just reading about it.

Marina at sunset always has a way of overdelivering — the sky doing its thing, the sun dipping low and gold, people scattered across the sand living out their evening. Add a horse into that frame and it stops being a photo and starts being everything a beach is supposed to feel like.
What caught me here wasn't the leaf itself, but how long it managed to hold onto the water — every droplet still clear, still clean, sitting there like it had no intention of falling anytime soon.

There's a look dogs give when they feel completely safe — and this was exactly that. A mother and her pup, playful and unguarded, right in front of the one human they trust most. You start to understand why "man's best friend" was never just a saying.
A second closer to the moment — no performance, no posing, just a mother and her pup leaning into each other the way only real trust allows.

There's something about a full moon that never misses — it just always looks picture perfect, glowing in that soft yellow it always seems to carry. And no matter how many times I look up, it's the same face looking back down. Never gets old, never gets less beautiful.

Another one from Rajasthan, and this time the frame did something the rest didn't — it pulled up a memory of Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani. That golden light slipping through the arches, the domes cutting into the sky — it's the kind of shot the movie made a whole aesthetic out of. Didn't plan it, just happened to be standing in the right spot at the right hour.

A watchtower standing right in the middle of a busy bazaar, stone carved to perfection — every tier, every bracket, every edge. Stood there looking up at it, life moving on below, wishing I could learn art the way people back then knew it. That kind of patience doesn't really exist anymore.

The Hawa Mahal — and honestly, it stopped me cold. Row after row of windows, each one carved with the same precision, built centuries before machines could've done it for them. Stunned by the beauty, stunned by the sheer civil engineering skill Indians had back then. Straight out of a history textbook, except this time I was standing right in front of it.

Almost missed him — an owl so camouflaged into the tree that he was practically part of the bark. Took a second look before I even realized he was staring right back. Makes you wonder if the beauty in an owl's eyes is just underrated, always hiding in plain sight like this.

Early morning out at sea, and it wasn't a tourist boat or a leisure ride — just fishermen going about the work that keeps them fed. No drama, no performance, just quiet labor against a colorless sky. Some frames don't need color to say something honest.

The Umaid Bhawan Palace in Jodhpur, all sandstone and dome, and right as I framed it a whole flock of birds decided to cut across the sky. Didn't plan that timing — just got lucky enough to catch history and life moving in the same shot.
A peacock, mid-stride, not performing for anyone — no feathers fanned out, no show. Just walking like it owns the ground beneath it. Didn't need the tail to look regal.

Rain again, and this one looked straight at me mid-call, antlers up, water running off him like it didn't matter. Behind him, a dark shape stood watching too — like the forest sent two very different animals to check who'd wandered in.

Not even in full bloom yet, still tightly wound in on itself, but framed against all that blurred green and gold, it looked like it already knew how good it was going to look later. Sometimes potential is the most photogenic thing there is.

Another corner of Rajasthan that made me stop and just look up. The carving under this chhatri is doing so much work — every bracket holding its own little sculpture — that the blue sky above almost felt like it was interrupting.

Just a deck of cards, cut and folded until the King and Queen of Hearts were holding hands over a heart of their own. Corny, maybe, but there's something sincere about turning something as ordinary as a playing card into a tiny love story.

Barely anything to see here, and that's kind of the point. Rain, one stubborn streetlight, and a road that disappears into the dark faster than you'd like. Some nights don't need detail to feel exactly like themselves.

Another temple spire, carved floor to peak without a single blank space left for rest. It's wild how something built centuries ago still manages to out-detail anything modern architecture attempts today.

The kind of corner in a Rajasthan palace where even the walls refuse to stay plain — every panel painted, every arch outlined, nothing left untouched. You could spend an hour on just this one wall and still miss half of it.

Long exposure, and the road turned into streaks of gold and red while the building in the back just sat there, lit up and unbothered. Everything moving, and one thing standing still — that contrast is what made me stop the car.

That same coast, this time at sunrise — the sun barely breaking through the clouds, setting the whole sky on fire before the day had even properly started. One tiny boat, riding the only strip of light on the water.

Jaisalmer's havelis don't do anything halfway — every balcony carved like lace, stacked one over another until the whole building looks like it's made of stone embroidery. Golden city earns its name honestly.
A crescent this time, not full — and somehow it felt even more dramatic than the full moon ever does. Half-lit, half-hidden, like it's only giving you part of the story on purpose.

The Asiatic lioness, Gir Forest — the only place on Earth you'll find her walking free like this. Calm, unbothered, completely in charge of her patch of jungle. You don't really understand "endangered and magnificent" until you're this close to one.
A closer look at the same lioness — every scar and whisker visible, that low growl practically audible through the photo. Beautiful, but she made sure you never forgot what she was.
One more from Gir — side profile, gold light catching every strand of that face. Didn't think a lioness without the mane could still look this commanding, but she did.

An abandoned room I wasn't even supposed to be photographing — wires hanging, walls stained, that one signboard still warning people to stay out. Some places hold onto their story even after everyone's left.
An empty parking structure at night, one lone car parked under the only working light. Quiet in a way that almost felt staged — like the whole place was waiting for someone to show up.
Late night, empty courtyard, one warm light doing all the work against the dark. Places look different once everyone else has gone to sleep — calmer, almost like they belong only to you.

An elderly woman, wrapped in a headscarf that told its own story before she said a word. Sat there with a stillness that looked earned — the kind you only get after decades of living exactly the way you wanted to.
McLeod Ganj at dusk, the mountains behind it doing that thing where they turn gold right before the light gives up for the day. Small hill town, big mountains — that scale never stops feeling unreal.
location: McLeod Ganj, Dharamshala, Himachal Pradesh, India

caption: A heron, patient and still, waiting by the water for a moment I never got to see happen. Sometimes the best part of wildlife photography isn't the catch — it's just watching something this calm do absolutely nothing.

Two figures, one canvas. Shiva on the left — trident in hand, the moon resting in his hair, calm the way only someone who's seen the end of everything can be calm. Parshuram on the right — axe raised, sky burning red behind him, wrath as devotion. Protector and destroyer, standing back to back. Held the painting over fire because that felt like the only honest way to shoot it.
